magadha:
[Maga+dhāvu+kvī]  CL=9 Maṃsa + gīdha + a. Magadha means 'those who run with the path' (magena saddhiṃ dhāvantīti magadhā). Alternatively, it means 'those who are greedy for flesh' (maṃsesu gijjhantīti vā magadhā). [References: Sī, Ṭī, Sac, 2. 300. Dhān, Ṭī. 184. Nīti, Dhā. 171. Maga + dhā + ka. Thoma. Maṇidīpa, 1. 239, 240 - also see.]
One who is called Magadha. (Magadha king, Magadha prince, Magadha citizen. In Amara, Sa, 18, 97 - it is also said to be one who praises and recites the royal lineage in front of the king).
See Magadha-(2). magadha Magadha (m) [Magadha + ṇa. In Sī, Ṭī, Sac, 2. 300 - it is said to be a rūḷhī word, and due to the elision of the taddhita suffix, there is no vuddhi in the Magadha word denoting the country. Ancient grammarians considered this word, like Kosala and Aṅga, to be either a taddhita word or a rūḷhī word, while Sanskrit grammar texts like Pāṇini consider it a rūḷhī word without proper etymology. (Mog, 4. 19 - see Sa note).]
In the Commentaries and Sub-commentaries, it is explained that the name "Magadha" comes from:
1. The words said to King Cetiya who was swallowed by the earth for speaking falsehood: 'Mā + gadhaṃ + pavisa' (Don"t enter hell).
2. The words said to those who were digging to find the king after he was swallowed: 'Mā + gadhaṃ + karotha' (Don"t dig a pit).
3. The words said to that king: 'Mā + ogadha' (Don"t sink into hell).
4. The words said to that king: 'Mā + katha' (Don"t speak falsehood).
Magadha refers to the country ruled by princes known as Magadha, the Magadha country. (Magadha is one of the 16 great countries (Aṅ, 1. 213. Aṅ, 3, 81). It is said in PEED to be the southern part of modern-day Bihar state in India).

The root [nāthadhātu] operates in four meanings:
1. [yācana] (requesting)
2. [upabhāpa] (causing distress/burning)
3. [issariya] (lordship/mastery)
4. [āsīsana] (wishing/aspiring)
The two roots [nātha] and [nādha] are established (in the texts).
The meanings of these roots are:
1. To wish for, to desire, to aspire
2. To cause burning (of defilements), to cause distress (to unwholesome states)
3. To request, to encourage, to rouse
4. To transcend, to overcome
5. To rule over, to have mastery, to have authority
